newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire opposition tilts at Prime Minister Kengo.
newsitem.headline: Zaire opposition tilts at Prime Minister Kengo.

text.p: Zaire's main political opposition said on Wednesday that its leader Etienne Tshisekedi would begin contacts soon on forming a government to negotiate with rebels advancing relentlessly in the east and south.
Heavy rain swept the capital Kinshasa where opposition militants showed no early sign of launching threatened protests to press for the sacking of Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
"Mr Tshisekedi should very soon be making contacts in order to form a government to negotiate with the rebels," Laurent Mbayo, a senior Tshisekedi adviser told Reuters.
With Kengo and ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko out of the country, Tshisekedi cancelled a planned news conference.

But in the absence of a constitutional successor to Mobutu in the event of his death or resignation, a debate raged within Zaire's political family over Kengo's future following a vote to oust him in the transitional parliament on Tuesday.

Supporters of Kengo, who was was in Kenya for regional talks on Zaire's war, and of Mobutu, who was in hospital in Europe, dismissed the vote as unconstitutional. They said it fell far short of a required two-thirds majority.
Government spokesman Jean Claude Biebie said the cabinet would meet on Wednesday to discuss the crisis. "I am not authorised to comment on it," he told Reuters.
"I would advise the prime minister to walk over this motion," Yezu Kitenge, minister of foreign trade and a close Mobutu associate, said.

But one Kengo ally said it would not be the first time in Zaire that a legally questionable vote became binding. "I think it is better for him to go this time. It might be dangerous to fight the desires of the people," the source added.
Opposition supporters say Kengo was elected as a compromise prime minister on just such a vote in 1994.

A March poll in Kinshasa suggested that 88.7 percent of the population had a bad opinion of Kengo, who is also a wealthy businessman. Many of Kinshasa's poor see him as a member of a ruling clique that has syphoned off the country's wealth.
A former opposition minister linked attempts to oust Kengo to deepening rifts with the military over the conduct of the war and related coup plots.

"It's true the military wanted to plan a coup. In their plan they would squeeze out Kengo in favour of another civilian candidate," former civil service minister Joseph Kanyonga of the Action Movement for the Resurrection of Congo (MARC) said.
He said civilians had been contacted last week about taking part in a coup. "Some officers did not want that. They wanted to take power to preserve Mobutism and to protect their interests."

He said there was still support for a coup but added that any coup would be short-lived. "If they go ahead with a military takeover it will be swept away soon afterwards and can only precipitate the arrival of the army of Kabila."
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila and his forces have named Kinshasa among their targets but remain a long way away.
Mobutu's son said from Europe, where the veteran president has spent most of his time since cancer surgery in August, that his father rejected any thought of talks with Kabila.
Under the interim constitution the head of the transitional parliament should succeed Mobutu. Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo resigned from the job in 1995 and has not been replaced.
A Mobutu supporter is one of the deputy speakers, an opposition supporter the other.
